preamble: The affrication of an aspirated alveolar stop [tʰ] to a postalveolar affricate [tʃ]. The clearest case is the English onset cluster /tr/, where the aspirated /t/ coarticulates with the following postalveolar approximant so that tree sounds like 'chree'. Magloughlin (2018) treats this as a coarticulatory effect that is being phonologized in North American English, and Bailey et al. (2022) document the same affrication in Manchester English. Speakers with a strongly retroflex /r/ produce a retroflex-like variant (see t_aspirated_to_ch_retroflex). An earlier version of this entry claimed Japanese ti > chi went through [tʰi]; Japanese has no aspiration contrast, so that case belongs under t_to_ch.

examples.note: Onset /tr/ affricates through coarticulation with the postalveolar approximant; heterosyllabic /t.r/ (rat-race) does not.
The same onset affrication; children's spellings such as 'chruck' reflect it.
Bailey et al. (2022) find /tr/ affrication and argue it drives the retraction of the preceding /s/.

sources: Magloughlin, L. (2018). /tɹ/ and /dɹ/ in North American English: Phonologization of a Coarticulatory Effect. PhD dissertation, University of Ottawa. https://doi.org/10.20381/ruor-21856
